title: Minestrone
subtitle: hearty Italian vegetable soup with pasta and beans
excerpt: Minestrone means 'big soup' in Italian, and it earns the name. This version uses whatever vegetables are in season, a tin of tomatoes, cannellini beans, and a handful of pasta. It is one of the most flexible soups you can make -- swap the vegetables to suit what you have.
sourceNotes: An Italian peasant soup with roots going back centuries. Every region of Italy has its own version. The word minestrone simply means 'large soup.'

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the pasta. Add freshly cooked pasta when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Make a big pot and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for 4 days. The pasta will absorb liquid -- add a splash of water when reheating.

content.text: Add the pasta in the last 10 minutes so it does not overcook. If you are making this ahead, cook the pasta separately and add it when serving.

items.prepNote: small shapes such as ditalini or broken spaghetti

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 8 minutes until soft.
Add the garlic and courgette. Cook for 3 minutes more.
Add the tinned tomatoes and stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes.
Add the cannellini beans and pasta. Cook for another 10 minutes until the pasta is tender.
Stir in the basil. Season with salt and pepper.
Ladle into bowls. Finish with a drizzle of olive oil and parmesan if using.

items.fix: Add more hot stock or water and stir well.

items.cause: Cooked too long in the soup
items.fix: Next time, cook pasta separately and add just before serving.

content.text: Minestrone has been made across Italy for hundreds of years. It started as a way to use whatever was growing or left in the kitchen. There is no single correct recipe -- it changes by region, season, and what is in the larder. This version follows the northern Italian style with beans and pasta.
